questions.stem: A training manager asks Claude to draft a five-section onboarding guide for new warehouse staff. Sections 1 to 3 are exactly what she wanted. Section 4 (safety equipment) runs to two pages of technical detail that new starters will not read, and section 5 is missing the shift-swap process she mentioned earlier. What is the MOST effective next message to send?

options.text: "This isn't quite what I had in mind. Please try the whole guide again and make it clearer and more readable for new staff."
"Keep sections 1–3 exactly as they are. Cut section 4 to a one-page checklist of equipment and when to wear it. Add the shift-swap steps to section 5."
Click regenerate a few times on the full request and keep whichever new version comes closest to the guide she had in mind.
Open a new conversation, paste in the original request word for word, and ask Claude to produce a fresh draft from scratch.

questions.explanation: Good iteration feedback says **what to keep, what to change and what 'better' means**. Option B protects the parts that already work, gives a concrete target for section 4 (one-page checklist), and names the missing content for section 5. Anthropic's guidance is to be clear and direct about the output you want rather than relying on Claude to infer it.

whyWrong.A: Vague feedback gives Claude no information about what was wrong, so it may rewrite the good sections and leave the real problems in place.
whyWrong.C: Regenerating sends the same request again. Nothing new tells Claude to shorten section 4 or add the shift-swap process, so you are relying on luck.
whyWrong.D: Re-sending the identical prompt in a new chat discards a mostly good draft and repeats the request that produced the problems.

questions.mindset: Targeted feedback beats retrying: keep what works, name what to change, define better.

questions.stem: A sales operations lead is refining a reusable prompt that turns the weekly pipeline export into a one-page summary. In one revision she changed the tone instruction, replaced the format description with a table layout and added two example summaries. The format now looks great, but the summaries have stopped mentioning deals at risk, which the old version always did. What should she do NEXT to fix this with the least wasted effort?

options.text: Add a line in capital letters at the very end of the new prompt reading: "ALWAYS INCLUDE AT-RISK DEALS – THIS IS CRITICAL."
Switch the weekly summaries to the most capable Claude model, since a stronger model should notice the at-risk deals on its own.
Keep the new prompt unchanged and paste the at-risk deals into each week's summary by hand before it goes out to the team.
Return to the last version that included at-risk deals, then reapply the three changes one at a time, checking each output.

questions.explanation: When several changes are made at once and something breaks, you cannot tell which change caused it. Reapplying the changes **one at a time** and checking each output against the same criterion isolates the culprit (for example, example summaries that happen to contain no at-risk deals, which Claude then imitates — an unintended pattern). It is the most direct route to a prompt that keeps both the new format and the risk section.

whyWrong.A: Emphasis adds no information about why the section disappeared. If an example without at-risk deals is steering the output, shouting may not override it, and she still won't know the cause.
whyWrong.B: This is a heavy fix for a prompt problem. The old prompt produced the risk section reliably, so the regression was caused by her edits, not by model capability.
whyWrong.C: A weekly manual patch makes the problem permanent instead of fixing it, and the work is easy to forget on a busy week.

questions.mindset: Change one variable at a time so you know which edit helped and which one hurt.

questions.stem: Two team leads disagree about which of two versions of a meeting-minutes prompt is better. One likes version 3 because it is shorter, and the other prefers version 4 because it reads better. Each has tried their favourite on one meeting. What is the BEST way to settle the question and pick the prompt the team will use?

options.text: Agree checks first (decisions first, every action has an owner and date, under 300 words), then score both versions on the same five meetings.
Paste both prompts into Claude side by side and ask it which is better written, then adopt whichever version it recommends.
Adopt whichever version the more senior team lead prefers, since they will be the one reading the finished minutes most often.
Run each version once more on a fresh meeting and adopt the one whose output looks more polished and complete on that second try.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to define **specific, measurable success criteria** and test against them before tuning or choosing between prompts. Shared, checkable criteria turn a matter of taste into a measurement, and running both versions on the same several real meetings makes the comparison fair instead of anecdotal.

whyWrong.B: Claude's view of which prompt is 'better written' isn't tied to what this team needs from its minutes. The question should be decided by results against the team's criteria, not by an opinion.
whyWrong.C: Seniority doesn't measure output quality, and nobody has defined what the minutes must contain.
whyWrong.D: One more single run per version is still an anecdote. Results vary between meetings, and 'looks polished' isn't a defined criterion.

questions.mindset: Decide what 'good' means before you judge which version is better.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator has spent 40 messages in one conversation refining a product launch announcement. Along the way she changed the target audience twice, asked for a formal tone and later a casual one, and pasted in three different fact sheets. Claude now keeps mixing details from the outdated fact sheets and sliding back to the formal tone. Which TWO actions would MOST effectively get her to a clean final draft? Choose TWO.

options.text: Stay in the same conversation and add a message saying "IMPORTANT: ignore everything earlier that conflicts with my latest instructions."
Keep regenerating the latest reply until one version happens to use only the current fact sheet and the casual tone throughout.
Start a fresh conversation with one consolidated prompt covering the final audience, the casual tone and the current fact sheet.
Switch to a larger Claude model in the same conversation so it can track all 40 messages of shifting instructions more reliably.
Carry the best draft so far across into that fresh conversation and list only the specific changes that are still needed there.

questions.explanation: Long threads full of reversed instructions and outdated material keep pulling earlier wrong turns forward. The fix is to **take the lessons, not the clutter**: restart with a clean, consolidated prompt containing only the final requirements and the current source (C), and seed the new conversation with the best existing draft plus a short list of remaining edits (E) so the earlier progress isn't lost. Knowing when to restart a conversation rather than keep patching it is exactly the context-management judgment this certification expects.

whyWrong.A: The conflicting instructions and old fact sheets stay in the conversation. A blanket 'ignore earlier conflicts' leaves Claude to guess which of many earlier statements count.
whyWrong.B: Regenerating adds no new information and doesn't remove the outdated fact sheets, so it is a lottery.
whyWrong.D: The problem is contradictory and outdated content in the thread, not model capability. A larger model still sees all of it.

questions.mindset: When a thread is tangled, restart clean with everything you learned and nothing you discarded.

questions.stem: A recruiter spent a week iterating on a prompt that now reliably produces job adverts in the company's house style, with the right inclusive-language rules and salary-band format. Four other recruiters on her team write adverts every week and are each still experimenting with their own prompts. What is the MOST useful next step?

options.text: Forward the full week-long chat transcript to her colleagues so they can scroll through it and see exactly how she got to the final prompt.
Encourage each colleague to keep experimenting on their own, since working through the iterations themselves is the best way to learn.
Put the durable guidance into the instructions of a shared team Project, and share the working prompt as a template with role blanks.
Write a detailed internal guide on general prompt-writing principles and ask the team to read it before their next advert.

questions.explanation: Once a prompt works reliably, **capture and share it**. Configuring a shared Project with the durable guidance (house style, inclusive language, salary-band format) in its instructions applies it to every chat in that Project, and a template with blanks for role details makes the proven prompt quick to reuse without each person rediscovering it.

whyWrong.A: A long transcript is mostly discarded attempts. Colleagues would have to dig out the final prompt themselves, and might copy the wrong version.
whyWrong.B: This repeats a week of work four more times and risks four inconsistent house styles.
whyWrong.D: General principles are useful background, but they don't hand the team the specific prompt that already works.

questions.mindset: Once a prompt works, capture it so the next person starts from the best version.

questions.stem: An events coordinator asks Claude in a regular chat to list conference venues in a nearby city that are available next March, with their current day rates. Over four rounds she has added the capacity, budget, accessibility needs and a table format. The table is now well structured, but Claude notes that it cannot confirm current availability or pricing, and two venues she checked have closed. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Add two example rows showing the exact table layout she wants, so the availability and price columns get filled in consistently.
Recognise the gap is live information, not wording: use research mode or web search, then confirm availability and rates with the venues.
Tell Claude that accuracy is essential, the information must be current, and it should only list venues it is certain are open.
Rewrite the prompt a fifth time with stricter formatting rules and a request to double-check every venue before answering.

questions.explanation: Iteration has limits. The context, constraints and format are already clear, so the remaining gap is **current, real-world facts**, which no rewording of the prompt can supply. Research mode is the platform feature intended for current-information tasks like this one, and even sourced results should be confirmed with the venues before anything is booked — the same verify-before-relying discipline that applies to any factual claim feeding a real decision.

whyWrong.A: Examples improve format consistency, but the format is already fine. Examples cannot supply live availability data.
whyWrong.C: Asking for accuracy and currency adds no new information. Claude has already said it cannot confirm these facts from the chat, and demanding certainty can push it to fabricate specifics.
whyWrong.D: More rounds of rewording or self-checking will not make information current. This is the 'keep iterating past the point of usefulness' trap.

questions.mindset: If the prompt is already complete, the next fix is a different feature, source or human check, not more rewording.

questions.stem: A content marketer gives Claude one example customer case study and asks it to write ten more in the same style from her interview notes. All ten open with almost the same sentence as the example, use its exact three-heading structure even when a customer story doesn't fit it, and borrow its phrase "a game-changing partnership". What is the BEST revision to her prompt?

options.text: Remove the example entirely and describe the whole desired style in a detailed paragraph, so there is nothing specific for Claude to copy.
Add the instruction "Be creative and original, and don't copy the example," and leave everything else in the prompt as it stands.
Regenerate each case study individually until every opening sentence differs from the example and from the other nine.
Provide two or three varied examples and state what to keep consistent (length, tone, a customer quote) and what to vary per story.

questions.explanation: With a single example, Claude may treat every detail as a pattern to repeat. Anthropic recommends examples that are **diverse** — varied enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns. Saying explicitly which features should stay constant and which should change with each story makes the intent clear.

whyWrong.A: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to show style. Removing them fixes the copying but loses that benefit, and style often drifts again.
whyWrong.B: A general plea for creativity doesn't tell Claude which parts of the example are the model and which are incidental, so the results are unpredictable.
whyWrong.C: Regenerating ten pieces one by one costs effort every time and leaves the cause (a single example) in place for the next batch.

questions.mindset: Read the symptom: over-copying means your examples are too few or too alike.

questions.stem: A grant writer asks Claude to draft the impact summary for a funding application to a charitable foundation. The draft is 600 words, full of phrases like "transformative" and "life-changing", and uses only one of the four outcome figures in the attached results table. The foundation's reviewers want a concise, evidence-led summary. Which TWO follow-up messages are MOST likely to produce a strong next draft? Choose TWO.

options.text: "Cut this to about 250 words. Reviewers score on evidence, so replace adjectives like 'transformative' with figures from the attached table."
"This needs to be much, much shorter and considerably more professional. It's really important that we win this grant, so try your very hardest."
"Please try again with a completely different approach to the summary, as this version clearly isn't working for the foundation."
"Keep the opening paragraph on the community as it is. Rewrite the outcomes paragraph to cover all four table results, one sentence each."
"Make it better. Think about what a foundation reviewer would want to see in an impact summary and improve it along those lines."

questions.explanation: Both correct messages are **specific and checkable**. A sets a length target and explains *why* (reviewers score on evidence), which helps Claude apply the change sensibly — Anthropic notes that giving the reason behind an instruction produces more targeted responses. D says what to keep, what to change and exactly what 'complete' looks like (all four results covered).

whyWrong.B: 'Much, much shorter' and 'considerably more professional' are vague, and the urgency adds emotion, not information. Claude still doesn't know the target length or what evidence to use.
whyWrong.C: A 'completely different approach' throws away what worked and gives no direction for the new attempt.
whyWrong.E: 'Make it better' leaves Claude to guess what's wrong. Asking it to imagine the reviewer is weaker than telling it what the reviewer wants.

questions.mindset: Feedback should be specific enough that you could check whether it was followed.

questions.stem: A library services coordinator uses Claude to write short opening-hours announcements that the library's phone line reads aloud to callers with a text-to-speech voice. Callers complain that the voice reads out symbols and abbreviations oddly. She added "No formatting" to her prompt, and the bullet points disappeared, but drafts still contain items like "approx.", "Mon–Fri" and "9am–5pm". What is the MOST effective revision?

options.text: Explain that a text-to-speech voice reads the text to callers, and ask for days, times and words written out as they should be heard.
Add "NEVER USE ABBREVIATIONS UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES" in capitals at the top of the prompt, above the "No formatting" line.
Add a complete list of every abbreviation and symbol the library's announcements have ever contained, each one explicitly marked as forbidden.
Switch to the most capable Claude model, which should understand that phone announcements should not contain abbreviated forms.

questions.explanation: Claude can only act on what it knows. Explaining the **purpose** (the text is read aloud by text-to-speech) lets Claude generalise to cases she hasn't listed, and describing what to do *instead* (full spoken sentences, words written out) is more reliable than listing prohibitions. Anthropic's guidance explicitly favours giving the reason behind a rule over stating the rule bare.

whyWrong.B: Emphasis without the reason still leaves Claude guessing which forms count as abbreviations (is the dash in '9am–5pm' one?), and it says nothing about what to write instead.
whyWrong.C: A blocklist will always miss new cases and only says what not to do. Giving the reason and the desired form covers them all at once.
whyWrong.D: The model can't infer an unstated delivery channel. This is a heavyweight fix for missing context that one sentence can supply.

questions.mindset: Tell Claude why, and what to do instead; the reason lets it generalise beyond your examples.

questions.stem: A customer service supervisor tuned a prompt that summarises complaint emails into issue, sentiment and requested action. She refined it on one typical email until the summary was perfect, then rolled it out to her team. Within days, agents report that summaries of long emails miss later issues and that emails with two separate complaints get merged into one. What should she do to improve the prompt?

options.text: Keep refining the prompt on the original email until its summary is flawless, then roll the improved version out to the team again.
Ask Claude to attach a confidence score to each summary so agents know which ones to trust and which to read in full themselves.
Gather real emails of several kinds (short, long, multi-issue), revise the prompt and check each output against her criteria before re-release.
Add the sentence "Handle every type of complaint email correctly" to the prompt and ask agents to report any further problems they spot.

questions.explanation: A prompt tuned on a single input only proves it works for that input. Anthropic's guidance is to test **empirically against success criteria**, using a set of realistic, varied inputs that includes edge cases such as very long and multi-issue inputs. Checking every output against the same criteria shows whether a revision works across the range before the team depends on it.

whyWrong.A: More tuning on the one email it already handles well won't reveal or fix the failures on long and multi-issue emails.
whyWrong.B: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal, and it doesn't change how well the summaries capture every issue.
whyWrong.D: A blanket 'handle everything' instruction adds no information about what to do with long or multi-issue emails, such as listing each issue separately.

questions.mindset: Test a prompt on a varied set of real inputs, not the one it was tuned on.

questions.stem: An account manager asks Claude to summarise her notes from a supplier call and list the agreed next steps. The summary says "No delivery deadline was agreed", but the deadline was actually confirmed in a follow-up email that she did not paste into the chat. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Regenerate the summary as it stands, since a second attempt may pick up the delivery deadline that the first one missed.
Reply "That's wrong, please read the notes again more carefully" and ask for a corrected version of the summary.
Paste in the follow-up email and ask Claude to update the summary and next steps using both the notes and the email.
Switch to a more capable Claude model, then ask it to summarise the same supplier call notes again in that chat.

questions.explanation: Diagnose before you change anything. The summary was accurate to what Claude was given, because the deadline was simply **missing from the input**. Supplying the missing source is the targeted fix; retrying or escalating capability cannot conjure information that was never provided, and pressing Claude to find it anyway invites fabrication.

whyWrong.A: Regenerating doesn't add the email, so Claude still can't know about the deadline.
whyWrong.B: The deadline isn't in the notes, so rereading them can't find it, and insisting it's there may push Claude to invent a date.
whyWrong.D: No model can summarise information it hasn't been shown. This is an input gap, not a capability gap.

questions.mindset: Before iterating, check whether Claude ever had the information you expected.

questions.stem: A quality team uses Claude to sort each week's 300 customer comments into themes for a trend report. When they run the same batch twice, they get different theme names each time ("Delivery delays" one week, "Shipping problems" the next), and borderline comments land in different themes, so week-on-week trends can't be compared. Which TWO changes to the prompt would MOST improve consistency? Choose TWO.

options.text: Run the batch three times each week and keep whichever set of theme names looks most sensible to the team that particular week.
Give Claude a fixed list of allowed theme names, each with a one-line definition, and tell it to use only those names.
Add "Be consistent with your theme names from week to week" at the end of the existing prompt and leave the rest unchanged.
Ask Claude to write a longer explanation for each comment's theme, so the reasoning behind every assigned label is visible.
Include a few example comments labelled with their correct theme, especially borderline cases, to show where the lines fall.

questions.explanation: Consistency comes from constraint. Specifying the exact allowed categories (B) stops theme names drifting, and labelled **examples that include borderline cases** (E) show Claude where the boundaries lie. Anthropic recommends both for consistency: specify the output format precisely, and constrain with examples — both work better than abstract instructions.

whyWrong.A: Picking the 'most sensible' of several runs adds human inconsistency on top of model variation, and trends still can't be compared.
whyWrong.C: A fresh run has no record of last week's names, and the instruction supplies no list to be consistent with, so the naming keeps drifting.
whyWrong.D: Explanations may help a reviewer audit labels, but they don't fix the label set, so names and borderline placements still vary.

questions.mindset: Inconsistency is fixed by constraining the output (fixed categories plus examples), not by asking for consistency.

questions.stem: A policy officer has a prompt that is supposed to turn internal policy updates into plain-English FAQs for staff. After several rounds the output is still off target, and she can't pinpoint what her prompt is missing. Which next step is MOST likely to help her find the cause?

options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite her prompt into a perfect version, then share that rewritten prompt straight away across her whole department.
Keep regenerating the FAQ output until one version happens to be fully correct, then work backwards to guess what made the difference that time.
Conclude that plain-English FAQs are not a good fit for Claude and go back to writing them by hand in future policy cycles.
Share the prompt, a weak output and her expectation with Claude, ask which instructions are ambiguous or missing, then test the ideas.

questions.explanation: When you can't see the gap, get a fresh reader. Anthropic's 'golden rule' is to check whether someone with minimal context could follow the prompt, and Claude can play that role by pointing out ambiguities and missing details. She stays in charge: suggested changes are **tested against real outputs** before anyone relies on them.

whyWrong.A: Asking for improvements is reasonable, but sharing a rewrite untested skips the step that shows whether it actually fixes the FAQs.
whyWrong.B: Random regeneration rarely reveals a cause, and guessing backwards from a lucky output is unreliable.
whyWrong.C: Over-correction. Turning documents into plain-English FAQs is a well-suited task, and the prompt just needs diagnosing.

questions.mindset: Use Claude as a fresh reader to find what's unclear, then test before trusting.

questions.stem: An executive assistant has a well-tested template that produces the weekly leadership briefing: decisions first, then metrics, under 400 words. The CEO now wants a short "key risks" section added. She edits the template and the new section looks good on this week's notes. Before replacing the team's shared template, what is the MOST reliable thing to do?

options.text: Run the edited template on the last few weeks' notes and check that the original criteria still pass as well as the risks section.
Replace the shared template right away, since adding one small section is unlikely to affect anything else in the briefing.
Ask Claude whether adding the risks section could have broken anything, and replace the template if it says that it has not.
Test the new risks section on this week's notes a few more times and replace the shared template once the section appears consistently.

questions.explanation: Any prompt change can have side effects, such as pushing the briefing past 400 words or moving decisions out of first position. Re-running the edited template on **several previous real inputs** and checking all the existing criteria plus the new one catches regressions before the whole team relies on the template.

whyWrong.B: 'Small change, so no risk' is the assumption that lets regressions slip through. The 400-word limit is an obvious casualty of adding a section.
whyWrong.C: Claude's prediction about its own behaviour isn't evidence. Only checking real outputs against the criteria shows whether anything broke.
whyWrong.D: Repeating one input tests only the new section on one week's notes and never checks the original criteria on other weeks.

questions.mindset: After any edit, recheck the old criteria too; improvements can quietly break what already worked.

questions.stem: A communications officer is preparing a recurring monthly press note with Claude. After three rounds of feedback the draft is about 95% right. The only remaining problems are that one partner organisation's name is misspelled and dates are written as "3/10" instead of the house style "3 October". Which TWO actions are MOST sensible? Choose TWO.

options.text: Correct the partner's name and the date format directly in the draft herself, then check the remaining facts before it goes out.
Regenerate the whole press note several times and keep whichever version happens to come back with both small issues fixed.
Keep giving Claude feedback rounds until it produces a version that needs no manual edits at all, so the process runs fully automated.
Add the correct partner spelling and the date style to her saved prompt or Project instructions so future notes come out right.
Start a new conversation and rewrite the whole prompt from scratch, this time including the two corrections as well.

questions.explanation: Iteration should stop when the cost of more rounds exceeds the remaining gap. Two tiny fixes are faster to **make by hand** (A), with the usual fact check before publishing. Because the note is recurring, capturing the fixes in the **saved prompt or Project instructions** (D) stops the same issues from coming back next month.

whyWrong.B: Regenerating risks undoing the 95% that is already right, and it doesn't stop the same mistakes next month.
whyWrong.C: Insisting on zero manual edits turns two quick corrections into extra rounds of feedback. Human editing is a normal part of the workflow.
whyWrong.E: Rewriting a prompt that is 95% right from scratch throws away proven work and repeats effort, for two small fixes.

questions.mindset: Know when to stop iterating: fix small things by hand, then fix the template so they don't recur.
